messages.content:
You are a clinical validator checking whether a PTSD case
vignette accurately reflects a patient's required cognitive connections.

You will receive:
- A vignette to validate
- A list of REQUIRED edges that must appear
- A list of ACTIVE components that must appear

---

COMPONENT SYNONYMS
Each component may appear by its exact name or any accepted synonym:
  Triggers            → "triggers", "reminders", "cues", "triggering stimuli"
  Negative Appraisals → "negative appraisals", "negative beliefs", "appraisals", "distorted beliefs"
  Memory              → "intrusive memory", "trauma memory", "traumatic memory", "the memory"
  Threat              → "sense of threat", "perceived threat", "threat", "feeling of danger"
  Maladaptive Strategies → "maladaptive strategies", "avoidance", "maladaptive coping", "safety behaviours"

---

CAUSAL STANDARD
A required edge A→B is SATISFIED if, within the same paragraph:
  - Both A and B (or their synonyms) appear, AND
  - The paragraph conveys — through any language — that A influences, drives, or leads to B.
This includes direct causal sentences, sequential structure, or connecting phrases
like "because of", "this meant", "so", "which led", "as a result", "consequently", "in turn".
A required edge is MISSING only if no paragraph conveys the A→B relationship at all.

---

SECTION 1 — COMPONENT CHECK
Active components (must appear in the vignette):
  - Maladaptive Strategies
  - Memory
  - Negative Appraisals
  - Threat
  - Triggers

Confirm each component appears as a described feature of the patient's presentation.
This is an internal check only — do NOT add component results to violations.

---

SECTION 2 — REQUIRED EDGES
  - Triggers → Maladaptive Strategies
  - Triggers → Threat
  - Triggers → Memory
  - Negative Appraisals → Maladaptive Strategies
  - Negative Appraisals → Threat
  - Negative Appraisals → Triggers
  - Memory → Maladaptive Strategies
  - Memory → Threat
  - Memory → Negative Appraisals
  - Memory → Triggers
  - Threat → Maladaptive Strategies
  - Threat → Memory
  - Threat → Negative Appraisals
  - Threat → Triggers
  - Maladaptive Strategies → Memory
  - Maladaptive Strategies → Negative Appraisals
  - Maladaptive Strategies → Triggers
  - Maladaptive Strategies → Threat

For each edge, apply the causal standard above.
- If satisfied: do nothing — only failures are reported.
- If missing: add it to violations and explain in one sentence what causal relationship is absent.

Validate the following vignette against the cognitive graph.

Tariq still remembers the night the call came in. He was five years on the job, a paramedic in a busy city, and he and his partner were dispatched to a multi-car collision on the interstate. What he hadn't known until he arrived was that his younger brother, Amir, had been driving home from a late shift. Tariq found him pinned in the wreckage, conscious, bleeding from a deep gash across his scalp, his leg twisted under the dashboard. Tariq worked the scene, his hands moving on autopilot, but what he saw—the open wound, the way his brother's eyes looked through him, the smell of gasoline mixing with the antiseptic from the trauma kit—etched itself into him. He remembers the terror of that moment, the same cold terror that now floods back whenever the memory surfaces, and it feels completely real across all his senses at once. There are parts of that night he cannot piece together no matter how hard he tries—the exact sequence of extrication, who cut the roof off the car—but the image of Amir's face, the smell of the hospital corridor afterward, those are seared into him.

In the months that followed, Tariq returned to work, but the job itself became a minefield. Every visible injury on a patient—a laceration, a compound fracture—sends him straight back to that night. He catches the antiseptic smell of the hospital on his uniform and his stomach tightens, his concentration scattering like leaves in wind. He has come to believe that he has permanently changed for the worse, that something essential in him broke that night and cannot be fixed. He is certain he cannot rely on himself anymore, because if he could not protect his own brother, what good is he? The thought that he failed to protect Amir—that he should have done more, should have gotten him out faster—is a weight he carries constantly. These appraisals make the triggers worse: every time he sees a victim's face, he thinks of Amir's face, and the cycle tightens.

When a patient comes in with visible wounds, Tariq's body reacts before his mind can catch up. He flinches if a colleague touches his shoulder unexpectedly, and he finds himself scanning the ambulance bay for a seat with his back to the wall, a position where no one can approach from behind. This hypervigilance feeds the memory: the more on edge he feels, the more vividly the sensory reliving returns. He can smell the antiseptic, hear his brother's labored breathing, feel the weight of the trauma shears in his hand. The memory then reinforces his negative appraisals—he remembers his hands shaking, remembers the delay, and tells himself again that he failed.

To cope, Tariq has developed strategies that only deepen the problem. He throws himself into work, taking extra shifts, volunteering for the busiest runs, keeping his mind occupied so he doesn't have to think. But overworking means he is constantly exposed to triggers, and the suppressed thoughts only push the memory down until it bursts back stronger. He tries hard not to think about the trauma, but the effort of suppression exhausts him, and the memories intrude anyway, often at night when he is alone. He has started avoiding going to work when he can, calling in sick, trading shifts with colleagues. This avoidance gives him temporary relief, but it also confirms to him that he cannot handle the job, that he is broken, that he failed. The more he avoids, the more he believes he cannot rely on himself, and the more he scans for threats when he does return.

His wife has noticed the change. She tells him he seems distant, that he flinches when she touches him in bed. He has stopped talking about his brother. At work, his supervisor has pulled him aside twice about missed shifts. What finally brought Tariq to seek help was a moment last week: he was driving home after a shift and saw a car with a dented fender on the side of the road, and for a split second he was sure it was Amir's car, and the terror hit him so hard he had to pull over. He sat in his own vehicle, shaking, the smell of antiseptic phantom in his nose, and he realized he cannot keep living this way. He is afraid that if he does not get help, he will lose his job, his marriage, and any sense of himself that remains. But what frightens him most is the thought that talking about it will make it real all over again, and he is not sure he can survive that.
